title: Private Types in Modules
story: Your library uses an internal cache structure. Users shouldn't touch it directly — they might corrupt it, or your future refactoring might break their code if they depend on it. Keep the type private, expose only safe operations.
why: Private types inside modules let you hide implementation details completely, exposing only safe, stable public functions that operate on them.
analogy: A vending machine's internal mechanism (private type) is hidden behind a metal panel. You interact through buttons (pub functions). The manufacturer can swap the internal mechanism without you ever noticing — same buttons, same drinks.
try_it: Try to access `c.count` directly from main — observe the compiler error. Then add a `pub fn decrement(c: &mut Tally)` that prevents going below zero. Add a `pub fn is_at_max(c: &Tally) -> Bool` to check if the counter is maxed out.
tips: Keep the type declaration in the module without `pub` to keep it private
Expose only functions that users need — start minimal, add more later
Private types let you refactor internals without breaking anyone's code
common_mistakes: Making types pub when they should be private — it's a permanent API commitment
Exposing raw field access instead of going through controlled functions
Not providing enough pub functions — users should be able to accomplish their goals
